fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lean Implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal: a Lean 4 implementation of Dependent Lambek Calculus whose surface syntax mirrors the on-paper presentation and elaborates, via Lean's extensible elaboration and metaprogramming, into the denotational semantics. The implementation should faithfully realize the full linear / non-linear calculus and be generic enough to evaluate the syntax in any category with sufficient structure — not solely the category of grammars.

Starting point. A Claude-written sketch lives in ~/grammars-and-semantic-actions/Lean/ (root LambekD.lean, elaborator under LambekD/Elab/, ~3.7k lines). It compiles and has working [| ... |] elaboration for the ordered linear fragment plus a grammar_inductive command. It is unaudited: the syntax/semantics correspondence and the design of the elaborator are not yet fully understood or owned. Treat it as scaffolding, not as a finished implementation.

html:ul.html:li: An elaboration pipeline from the on-paper Lambek^D syntax into Lean terms that I understand end-to-end and can extend.
An embedded DSL for the full linear / non-linear calculus (not just the ordered linear fragment).

An abstraction of the elaborator over the target category, so that the same surface syntax can be interpreted in any sufficiently structured category — recovering the grammars instance as one example.

fr:title.text: How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: How the LinearElab Elaborator Compiles to Category-Polymorphic Morphisms

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Intuitive walkthrough of Lean/LambekD/LinearElab/ — how a surface term like

gets turned into a morphism \llbracket {A \otimes B}\rrbracket _\ell \to A \otimes B in an abstract monoidal / biclosed / (co)cartesian / indexed / inductive category \mathcal {C}. Meant to be read alongside the code, not as a spec.

fr:title.text: The big picture

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The elaborator is a syntax-to-syntax preprocessor. It does not manufacture Lean Exprs itself; instead it reads a DSL expression, decides for each subterm which typed combinator should stand in for it, and builds a Lean source-level term that applies those combinators. The generated source is handed back to Lean's normal elabTerm at the very end. Unification, typeclass resolution, and universe inference happen once, there, on the full tree — not piecewise while we are walking the DSL.
Conceptually:

html:ul.html:li: DSL syntax (category lterm) lives in LinearElab/Syntax.lean. Each connective of the paper has its own shape: (x, y), let (a,b) = _ in _, fun (x:A) =>, ⟨e₁, e₂⟩, match _ with | inl a => _ | inr b => _, and so on.

Combinators live in LambekD.Linear.{Monoidal,Biclosed, Cartesian,Cocartesian,IndexedProducts,IndexedCoproducts,Inductive}. Each is a plain Lean definition parametric in a category \mathcal {C} carrying only the structure that connective needs (monoidal, left- closed, right-closed, chosen products, chosen coproducts, chosen distributor, initial algebras). No reference to Grammar.

The elaborator in LinearElab/Elaborator.lean is the bridge: one partial def per DSL form, emitting a TSyntax `term that mentions exactly the right combinator with exactly the right context arguments pinned down.

fr:title.text: What the combinators want from us

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What the combinators want from us

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Take tensorIntro as representative:
tensorIntro (e₁ : ⟦Δ⟧ₗ ⟶ A) (e₂ : ⟦Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ B) : ⟦Δ ++ Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ A ⊗ B (with Δ, Δ', A, B implicit).

LinCtx C is an ordered left-to-right list of \mathcal {C}-objects (think: a telescope of linear types). ⟦_⟧ₗ folds it into a right-nested tensor. The combinator takes two morphisms, on contexts Δ and Δ', and returns a morphism on the concatenated context Δ ++ Δ'.

So when the user writes (e₁, e₂) with ambient context \Delta _{\text {full}}, there is exactly one decision to make: where to cut \Delta _{\text {full}} into a prefix \Delta used by e₁ and a suffix \Delta ' used by e₂. The rest — what A, B, and \mathcal {C} are — is Lean's problem.

Every other combinator is the same pattern. Some take one context (var, unitIntro, prodIntro, sumInl); some take a middle slice and an outer prefix + suffix (unitElim, tensorElim, sumElim, coprodDElim, botElim); the rest are binders that add or remove a single slot at the front or the end (limpRIntro, limpLIntro, funD). The elaborator's job is to look at the DSL shape, compute the cuts, and emit the corresponding combinator applied to its inputs with the cuts threaded through explicitly.

fr:title.text: The cutting algorithm: free variables and ordering

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The cutting algorithm: free variables and ordering

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two tiny helpers do almost all the work.

html:ul.html:li: freeVars : TSyntax `lterm → Array Name — purely syntactic, recurses through the term and collects identifiers that are not shadowed by a binder. It knows about all the DSL's binding forms (let () = _ in, let (a,b) = _ in, fun (x:T) =>, funl (x:T) =>, match _ with | inl a | inr b, matchD _ with | ⟪x, y⟫).

splitCtx fvLeft fvRight — walks the ambient context left-to-right and finds the unique split point i such that the first i names lie in fvLeft and the rest in fvRight. Throws an error if any variable is unused, reused across branches, or appears out of order.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For middle-slice forms (let (a,b) = e in e' and friends) there is a second helper splitCtxMiddle fvMid fvOuter that finds a contiguous range of indices all of whose variables lie in fvMid, asserts that range really is contiguous, and returns the three pieces \Delta '_1, \Delta , \Delta '_2 around it.

These two functions enforce ordered linearity — no contraction (variable appearing twice on the same side of a split), no weakening (a variable that goes nowhere), no exchange (a left-variable appearing after a right-variable). When the user-written binder structure of the DSL does not support a valid cut, splitCtx itself raises the error. The main loop never has to think about linearity; it only asks "where does the cut go?" and delegates.

Cartesian and indexed-product intro are the only forms that do not cut: ⟨e₁, e₂⟩ shares the whole ambient context between the two branches (cartesian is additive, so it permits the same resources to be used by both). The elaborator simply recurses on each branch with the full ctx and lets the branches' internal linearity checks enforce that each branch really does consume it.

fr:title.text: The unification subtlety — why we pin Δ with named arguments

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The unification subtlety — why we pin Δ with named arguments

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Combinators like tensorIntro type as ⟦Δ ++ Δ'⟧ₗ ⟶ A ⊗ B. When we apply such a combinator to a concrete ambient context \Delta _{\text {full}}, Lean's unifier tries to solve Δ ++ Δ' = Δ_full. That equation has many solutions (any cut point works), and because LinCtx.append recurses on its right argument, Lean's unifier eagerly pins \Delta ' to some small suffix and leaves \Delta as whatever is left — typically not the split our FV analysis computed.
To stop Lean from guessing, the elaborator serialises the exact cut pieces back into surface syntax:

html:p.html:code: ctxToSyntax vars = nil.snoc A₀.snoc A₁. ⋯ .snoc A_k

fr:mainmatter.html:p: and passes them to the combinator as named implicit arguments ((Δ := $Δstx) / (Δ' := $Δ'stx)). Now when Lean sees tensorIntro (Δ := A,B) (Δ' := C,D) m₁ m₂, both halves are syntactically pinned and the equation (A,B) ++ (C,D) = A,B,C,D reduces definitionally. No unification ambiguity remains.
The same trick is what unblocks middle-slice combinators (unitElim, tensorElim, sumElim, coprodDElim, botElim), which have two append patterns in their types.

fr:title.text: Per-connective intuitions
Monoidal (the skeleton)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: x ⟶ Linear.var A: singleton context [(x, A)] maps by identity into the slot.
() ⟶ Linear.unitIntro: requires empty context, produces the monoidal unit I.
(e₁, e₂) ⟶ tensorIntro (Δ := …) (Δ' := …) m₁ m₂: splitCtx (FV e₁) (FV e₂) picks the cut; each branch is elaborated in its own piece of the context.

let () = e in e' and let (a,b) = e in e': e consumes a middle slice Δ, e' runs on Δ'₁ ++ Δ'₂ (plus the new binders in the pair case). We emit unitElim / tensorElim with the three pieces pinned. The new binders in the pair case get hole types _; Lean fills them from the type of e.

fr:title.text: Biclosed (binders)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Ordinary functions come in two flavours because context is ordered. fun (x : A) => e pushes x onto the end of the ambient ctx and emits limpRIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing A →[C] B. funl (x : A) => e pushes it onto the front and emits limpLIntro (Δ := ambient) body, producing B [C]← A. The ambient ctx is passed as Δ so that Lean does not try to solve Δ.snoc A = newCtx or sole A ++ Δ = newCtx by guessing.

Application likewise splits into two rules by which side the function appears on. f a (juxtaposition, function on the left) is limpRApp; a ·⟜ f (argument on the left) is limpLApp. The two combinators have their append patterns in opposite orders (Δ ++ Δ' vs Δ' ++ Δ), so the elaborator has to know which side is the function when it emits the call.

fr:title.text: Cartesian (⟨⟩, ⟨e₁, e₂⟩, π₁, π₂)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Additive, so there is no cut: ⟨e₁, e₂⟩ elaborates both branches under the same ambient context, and Lean's A \amp B constructor uses the cartesian lift combinator. ⟨⟩ is the unique morphism into the chosen terminal and accepts any ambient ctx. Projections just post-compose with fst or snd.

fr:title.text: Cocartesian (inl, inr, match, absurd)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Injections are pre-composed with inl / inr — no cut.

match e with | inl a => f | inr b => g is the only genuinely subtle monoidal case outside tensor-elim. The scrutinee e consumes a contiguous middle slice \Delta , and both branches share the outer context \Delta '_1, \Delta '_2, each extending it with one new binder (a or b, with hole types filled from e's type). Emission is sumElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m mf mg; the underlying combinator bakes in the distributor so that the two branches of the coproduct really do glue back into a single morphism on the whole ambient ctx.

absurd e is \bot -elim. The scrutinee provides a morphism into the initial object; the distributor's annihilation maps any flanking context to the initial. That means we are allowed to have ambient variables that do not appear in e at all — they just get annihilated. In freeVars this breaks the usual "every variable must be used somewhere" invariant, so the elaborator special-cases absurd: ambient vars outside FV(e) are treated as "used by the annihilation", not as an unused-variable error.

fr:title.text: Indexed products and coproducts (non-linear binders)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: funD (x : X) => e introduces a non-linear (Lean-level) binder x : X that the body can mention as an ordinary Lean term but not as a linear variable. The linear context is unchanged for the body — nothing is consumed. The elaborator elaborates e under the same ambient ctx, then wraps the result in a Lean fun x : X => _ and hands that to prodDIntro, which is exactly the liftD of the chosen indexed-product structure.
e ·@ x post-composes the projection at index x.
⟪x, e⟫ injects at a specified index; coprodDInj x e.

matchD e with | ⟪x, y⟫ => body: like match, e consumes a middle slice and body gets one new linear binder y (with a hole type inferred from the index family) and one non-linear binder x : X. Emission is coprodDElim (Δ'₁ := …) (Δ := …) (Δ'₂ := …) m (fun x => body), where the fun x => … captures the non-linear binder from the surface syntax.

fr:title.text: Initial algebras (roll, fold)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: roll[x] e is muRoll _ x e, which is literally e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.roll x: post-compose the linear body with the initial algebra's constructor at index x. The _ is a placeholder for the functor F, which Lean is expected to recover from the expected return type \mu F x.

fold[algs] e is muFold algs e = e ≫ HasInitialAlgebra.fold algs x: post-compose with the catamorphism induced by the algebra algs : ∀ y, (F y).denote A ⟶ A y. roll and fold do not restructure the context; they just chain on top of it.

The \beta and \eta laws of initial algebras (fold_roll, fold_unique) are semantic lemmas, not judgmental — the elaborator does nothing to expose them, it is up to the programmer to rewrite when needed.

fr:title.text: Entry point: the DSL brackets

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The top-level macro in elabLinearBracket:

html:ol.html:li: Reads the surface syntax (x₁ : A₁) … (xₙ : Aₙ) => body.
Builds the initial ElabCtx from the typed binders: an array of (Name × TSyntax `term) pairs, in the order written.

Runs the elaborator elabLTerm body under that context. The output is a single TSyntax `term — a Lean source-level term mentioning Linear.tensorIntro, Linear.sumElim, etc., with all context pieces and non-linear binders wired up.

Calls Lean.Elab.Term.elabTerm on that syntax with the expected type from the surrounding Lean context. Unification and typeclass resolution — for the category \mathcal {C} itself, for the types of the binders, for the appropriate chosen-structure instances — all happen here, once, on the finished tree.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The elaborator never inspects Expr, never calls isDefEq, never synthesises an instance. It is a syntactic preprocessor that knows how to name the right combinators and pin their context implicits; everything semantic is Lean's job.

fr:title.text: What is not there (yet)

html:ul.html:li: No escape hatch #[f] to embed a Lean-level morphism. The grammar-specific Elab/ elaborator has one; the linear one does not — if you need to use a Lean-constructed morphism, you must currently write the term directly (as in the prodDIntro smoke test which falls back to the raw combinator).
No constructor-apps for grammar_inductive-style named data. The inductive surface here is only the roll/fold pair.
No match … with on μ F beyond what fold expresses, and no equivalent of the grammar_decreasing termination plumbing. Both were grammar-specific in the older elaborator.
No Lean-level rewrite / simp hooks; β/η laws of each connective exist as simp lemmas on the combinators, but the DSL does not surface them.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are all deliberate omissions — the LinearElab elaborator is the minimal, category-polymorphic core. The grammar-specific pieces live in the older Elab/ tree and compose with these combinators via instances on Grammar.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Well-Founded Recursion in Dependent Lambek Calculus

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The goal is to understand how well-founded (recursive) coalgebras can be expressed or internalized in the dependent Lambek calculus. The motivating question is whether a syntactic guarded modality can serve as a principled mechanism for well-founded recursion in the calculus, with the recursive coalgebra characterizations from [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] as a guide.

fr:title.text: The negative fixed point, μ=ν coincidence, and Löb

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The negative fixed point, μ=ν coincidence, and Löb

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The reduct puts a \nu on the refutation side. Three questions decide whether refutations are computable: does \nu F^- exist, is it inductive, and can refute be built by guarded recursion?
Existence is now library fact: Grammar.Coinductive.Indexed provides \nu , corec, and finality on the box branch — the prerequisite flagged in sss-00BQ is discharged.

The 
u is canonical; \mu is sometimes a bonus. The consistency argument of sss-00EU recurses only along the finite parse tree, so even infinitely deep refutations are sound. And 
u is semantically necessary: for the unguarded A = \mu X.\, X =  ot (the empty grammar), F^- = X^- gives \mu X^-. X^- =  ot — no refutations, totality fails — while 
u X^-. X^- = 	op is the true complement, inhabited everywhere by the constant corec. Initial/final coincidence must therefore be treated as a fragment privilege, never a pipeline assumption.

In the guarded fragment, coincidence upgrades refutations to certificates. For locally contractive functors, initial algebra and final coalgebra coincide; if F^- is locally contractive at the suffix (or span) order, then \nu X^-. F^- = \mu X^-. F^-: refutations are finite, and refute is a fold. This is the reduct's consumer of the CCL coincidence machinery (sss-00EF, items 1 and 6). Outside the fragment, refute is built by corec instead, and totality may still hold coinductively (as in the \mu X. X example: \mathsf {inr} \circ \mathsf {corec}). Negation-containing F (Liar-style, genuine outer \mu ^i) never has a coincidence to hope for.

Caution — guardedness does not transfer for free. Dualising \otimes \mapsto \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} changes where recursion sits: in Dyck's F^- = \mathsf {NES} \mathrel {\And } (\neg \mathsf {lit}(a) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^- \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} \neg \mathsf {lit}(b) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^-), the \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} quantifies over all splits, including degenerate ones that place X^- at the full string (padding other factors with \varepsilon ). So an F^--refutation may choose an unguarded disjunct; productivity is by choice, not by shape. The lemma to prove: if F is Guarded (in the CodeGuarded sense), then F^- is locally contractive — plausibly via \mathsf {NES} forcing progress on the split that matters — but it is a genuine lemma, not an inheritance. sss-00BQ's claim that "the negative recursion is well-founded by string length" is exactly this obligation.

Löb builds refute. Once F^- is locally contractive, refute : \StringGram \vdash A^- \oplus \top -shaped producers arise by lob exactly as parsers do — the a2c (corecursive-algebra) half of the bilateral stack is the formal dual of Theorem 3.7, and the \rhd -guarded fixpoint supplies its productivity. Both halves run off one well-foundedness proof and one shared Brzozowski coalgebra.

fr:title.text: Atkey's reduct as a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra stack

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Atkey's reduct as a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra stack

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Synthesis tying Atkey's data types with negation and the GL-reduct route to complement grammars to the recursive-coalgebra framework of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] that underwrites the derivative-based CFG parser plan and Cass's claim that (\mu F)^{-1} is always recursive.

fr:title.text: The bridge

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Cass–Urbat–Wißmann picture: an intrinsically correct algorithm is the unique c2a-morphism from a recursive coalgebra (C, \gamma : C \to FC) to an algebra (A, \alpha : FA \to A). For a parser, the algebra is \mu F^+ and the coalgebra is the input string with derivative structure. Parse is intrinsically correct because it is unique. This is a purely positive story.
Atkey's reduct is the bilateral generalisation. The doubled fixed point
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: D \;=\; \mu ^i Y.\;{\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\;\nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: forces a \mu on the positive side and a \nu on the negative side. The two sides have dual recursion principles, which already exist in the literature as the two halves of Capretta–Uustalu– Vene:

html:ul.html:li: Positive. Initial algebra \mu F^+; recursion principle is recursive coalgebra (CUV 2006). Style: catamorphism / fold / well-founded. Computes a parse tree.
Negative. Terminal coalgebra \nu F^-; recursion principle is corecursive algebra (CUV 2009). Style: anamorphism / unfold / productive. Computes a refutation trace.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So the reduct is a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra bialgebraic construction, doubly nested: an outer \mu ^i in \mathbf {Chu}^i parameterising an inner \mu on the positive side and an inner \nu on the negative side. Each layer has a known universal property. None of this is new — what is new is that putting them together gives complement grammars under recursion.

fr:title.text: Cass's lever fires twice

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cass's claim: the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, regardless of whether it is the final coalgebra. Apply it twice in the reduct stack:

html:ul.html:li: Inner positive. D^+ = \mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-) (with Y^- fixed) is an initial algebra. Its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow structural recursion on parse trees works without step-indexing or guarded modalities.

Outer \mu ^i. The outer fixed point is an initial algebra in \mathbf {Chu}^i. By the same lemma — lifted to \mathbf {Chu}^i, which needs a separate check — its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow recursion on the stage of knowledge Y is well-founded.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dually, the standard CUV theorem the inverse of a terminal coalgebra is a corecursive algebra fires on the negative side, giving productivity for refutation generation. So the negative half also avoids guarded modalities, again contingent on the lemma transporting to our setting.

fr:title.text: Fit with the derivative-based CFG parser plan

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Fit with the derivative-based CFG parser plan

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Phases 1–6 of sss-00A3 build the positive half: CFGDesc defines F^+; Brzozowski derivatives define an input coalgebra \mathsf {String} \to \hat {F}\, \mathsf {String}; the parser is the unique c2a-morphism into D^+ = \mu F^+.
Adding the Chu partner D^- is the same shape of work, dualised:

html:ol.html:li: Compute F^- from CFGDesc by walking the syntax (this is the GL reduct on the grammar description).
Set D^- = \nu F^-, the terminal coalgebra of refutations.
The refutation function is the unique a2c-morphism out of the same input coalgebra \mathsf {String} \to \hat {F}\, \mathsf {String}, into D^-.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The input coalgebra is shared. Brzozowski's derivative just decomposes the input — it does not commit to a direction. Both the c2a-fold (parse) and the a2c-unfold (refute) consume the same derivative coalgebra. The Chu pair (\mathsf {parse}, \mathsf {refute}) is two morphisms with a common source.

Totality \StringGram \vdash D^+ \oplus D^- is then a theorem about the two morphisms — that they partition input space — not a part of the construction itself. Provable for decidable fragments (LL(k), DCFL like Dyck), not provable in general.

fr:title.text: What the synthesis pays for

html:ul.html:li:
Refutations get a universal property. Currently A_
eg is hand-built (rejecting DFA traces) with no categorical relation to the positive grammar. The reduct + corecursive algebra view makes A_
eg the unique a2c-morphism into 
u F^- — the negative twin of parse is the unique c2a-morphism into \mu F^+.

Correctness decoupled from termination, both sides. Cass already separates correctness (uniqueness) from termination (well-foundedness of the coalgebra) on the positive side. The reduct buys the same separation for refutations: correctness from uniqueness of the a2c-morphism, productivity from the same input coalgebra being well-founded.

Guarded modalities become optional for parsing. The guarded modality work and \rhd -Löb induction need not be the well-foundedness mechanism for parsing decidable CFGs — Cass's lever and its dual suffice. Guards remain the right tool for genuinely non-well-founded scenarios (streaming, infinite languages).

Same machinery as the existing plan. The CFGDesc, derivatives, and well-founded-on-string-length recursion already needed for the positive side carry over verbatim to the negative side under duality. There is no new infrastructure needed beyond restoring final coalgebras to the codebase.

fr:title.text: Later Operator ▶ as Internalised Guard

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The plan is self-contained without any modalities: productivity is a side condition on CFGDesc, nullability is an external decision sss-00A5, and well-foundedness is operational recursion on length sss-00A8. A later operator ▶ would internalise each of these into the type system, making the same construction fall out of guarded fixpoint rather than a sequence of external theorems.
Two natural slots for ▶:

html:p.html:strong: 1. As the guard on μ in CFGDesc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The current productivity condition on CFGDesc ("every self-reference sits under a non-nullable prefix") is a bespoke later modality indexed by "must consume ≥1 char." First-class ▶ replaces the side condition with a syntactic requirement:

where F is any unconstrained CFGDesc-style functor. This is exactly the trade-up that the Grammar.SequentialUnambiguity.Nullable scaffolding already gestures at: ¬Nullable A is a proposition about a grammar; ▶ would be a grammar constructor.

The paper's guard functor (F ↓₀) X i = F (λ j → (j ≺ i) × X j) i is already a parameterised later modality: the parameter is the well-founded relation ≺, not a global clock. So the machinery in IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs.lagda is morally a per-index ▶, and moving to a syntactic ▶ is just factoring that indexing into the type theory.

html:p.html:strong: 2. As the meaning of A ⟜ char c.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Recall from ⟜-as-derivative that
(A ⟜ char c) w = A (c ∷ w),

i.e. inhabiting A ⟜ char c requires being fed one character before producing an A. This is the defining behaviour of a later modality: availability delayed by one step, where "step" = "one character consumed."
Under this reading the Brzozowski identity char c · A ≅ δ c A becomes an applicativity law:
char c · (A ⟜ char c) ⊢ A (▶-apply)
and the derivative-based parser is a guarded fixpoint:

html:p.html:code: parse : μ self. (char? ⟜ ε ⊕ (Σ c. ▶ (parse (δ c G))))

fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the self-reference is guarded by ▶ ≡ (_ ⟜ char c), and the well-foundedness witness F-ε⁻¹ of c2a-morph is exactly the "take a later and cash it in" rule.

html:ul.html:li: Nullability becomes decidable by typing. ε ⊢ A iff A is ▶-free at the outer layer; no external decision needed.
Length-well-foundedness becomes automatic. Each ▶-unfold consumes exactly one character, so recursion depth ≤ input length by construction. sss-00A8's use of <-wellFounded disappears.

c2a-morph becomes guarded fixpoint. The paper's uniqueness theorem specialises to the Löb-style uniqueness of guarded fixpoints in the appropriate topos. Computational content is the same; meta-theory is cleaner.
Not on the critical path. The plan works without ▶; this tree is about a cleaner re-foundation, not a missing step.

Integration cost. Adding ▶ as a primitive means revisiting every grammar operation (tensor, residual, fixed points) to specify its interaction with ▶. Feasible, but a larger design commitment than "a few side conditions."

Which ▶? Classical guarded type theory's ▶ is character-agnostic (one "tick" per step). Ours is character-indexed (▶_c A = A ⟜ char c). The paper's (F ↓₀) sits in between — indexed by an abstract ≺. Whether to use a single ▶ or a character-indexed family is itself a design question.

html:ol.html:li: Prototype ▶ A as an alias for Σ c : Alphabet. A ⟜ char c (character-indexed form) inside the existing calculus, without new primitives.
Re-state nullability as a syntactic check on ▶-absence at the top of a description.
Re-derive c2a-morph for the single-step case and see whether the ▶-elimination rule does the work currently done by F-ε⁻¹.
Only then consider adding ▶ to CFGDesc as a primitive constructor (step 1 of sss-00A4).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open: does a character-indexed ▶ compose into a single modality after applying the "erase the character" projection? That would bridge the specific (Brzozowski-style) and generic (Löb-style) readings.

fr:title.text: Risks and Open Questions — Derivative-Based CFG Parser

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Risks and Open Questions — Derivative-Based CFG Parser

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Risks for the plan, ordered by how likely they are to cause rework.

html:ul.html:li: Productivity of μ in CFGDesc. The non-nullable-prefix condition is the natural guardedness criterion, but formalising it compositionally (so all constructors preserve it with reasonable evidence) is not obvious. A too-strict condition rules out Dyck; a too-loose one fails to give well-founded derivatives.

Derivative descriptions on μ. Unfolding under δ is the standard trick, but in a strongly-typed setting we have to show that the unfolded description is again a legal CFGDesc (productivity preserved). Might need to enrich CFGDesc with a rec or ν constructor that tracks the "unfolded state".

Nullability gate interacting with ⟜. The Brzozowski rule δ c (G · H) = δ c G · H ⊕ ν? G · δ c H uses classical disjunction. In Lambek we need the grammar-level iso c · (G · H) ≅ (c · G) · H + [G is ε-derivable] · (c · H); the second summand is zero when G is non-nullable. Check that the ⟜-as-derivative framing still composes cleanly through this case distinction.

c2a-morph at Type vs Set. The intrinsically-recursive paper is formalised in Set^I. Grammars in this project are String → Type. The constructions look generic over the universe, but there may be isSet obligations (or propositional-truncation issues) hidden in the uniqueness proof. See parser as c2a-morphism.

Infinite state space. For CFGs the reachable derivatives of a grammar are unbounded. We don't need finitely many descriptions, but we do need each derivative to be well-typed and computable. The danger is that our description type is not closed under δ — i.e., δ produces something outside CFGDesc. This has to be proven, not just asserted.

Coalgebraic "parsing" framing vs Parser record. Cass's Automata.Deterministic.parseNatTrans is a natural transformation between the word functor and the trace functor — a genuine coalgebraic object — but it gives a DFA-shaped coalgebra that doesn't obviously subsume our Parser A B return type. We may need to compose their NT-style result with a decide step on the final state to recover A ⊕ B. Not blocking, but a loose end.

Constructive negation of CFG. ¬ ⟦ G ⟧cfg w is what Parser wants on the reject side, but in general the negation of a CFG membership predicate is not itself a CFG. We will be inhabiting a proof of non-membership, not a grammar. Worth confirming that the disjointness obligation disjoint A B is satisfied by this formulation.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Validation milestone: implement hand-rolled Dyck parser end-to-end, before generalising to CFGDesc. Concrete failure modes surface much faster at the semantic level.

fr:title.text: Parser as Unique c2a-Morphism of a Recursive Coalgebra

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parser as Unique c2a-Morphism of a Recursive Coalgebra

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal: reinterpret the length-recursive parser as the unique coalgebra-to-algebra morphism produced by the c2a-morph construction of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] (file IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs.lagda, module c2a.c2a-morph).
Concretely we need to supply five pieces:

html:ol.html:li: A carrier C : ℕ → Type (indexed by input length). The coalgebra input at length n is the set of strings of that length paired with the current derivative state G.
A well-founded relation on ℕ: the standard _<_, with well-foundedness from Cubical.Induction.WellFounded.
A base endofunctor F on ℕ → Type expressing one character of progress: F X n = nullability-answer-at-0 ⊕ (Alphabet × X (n-1)).
The well-foundedness witness F-ε⁻¹ : F X n ⊢ (F ↓₀) X n coming from the fact that every recursive occurrence sits under a strictly-decreasing length.
A coalgebra c : C ⇒ F C (one step of derivative) and an algebra a : F Answer ⇒ Answer, where Answer G w = Parser ⟦ G ⟧cfg (¬ ⟦ G ⟧cfg) w.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Applying c2a.c2a-morph to these yields a morphism parse : C ⇒ Answer together with the uniqueness property inherited from the recursive-coalgebra framework. Uniqueness is exactly the statement that "the parser is the correct parser" — there is only one coalgebra-to-algebra morphism, so any alternative definition agrees with ours on every input.
Contrast with the intrinsically-recursive GCD and CYK:

html:ul.html:li: GCD is well-founded on proj₂ of ℕ × ℕ. Ours is well-founded on length of the string — the same idea (project down to ℕ, use <).

CYK uses List⁺ to sidestep nullability entirely. We cannot do that — nullability is a first-class question for CFGs — but we handle it by threading the nullability decision through the algebra at length 0.
Both GCD and CYK pay the price of defining the base functor and its well-foundedness lemma by hand. Ours pays the same price uniformly, parameterised over G : CFGDesc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open: does c2a-morph give us extensional uniqueness (the thing we want, since grammars are propositions at each string), or does it give a stronger computational equality? IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs proves unique.unique at the indexed-set level; check whether its use of Set-level equalities causes friction with our Type-valued grammars. Tracked in risks.

fr:title.text: Parser by Well-Founded Recursion on String Length

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parser by Well-Founded Recursion on String Length

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We want a generic parser
for every G : CFGDesc, where Parser A B (from Parser.Base) packages a splitting string ⊢ A ⊕ B with a disjointness witness disjoint A B.
Construction, by induction on input length:

html:ol.html:li: If the input is ε, answer by decidable nullability: G is nullable ⟹ inhabit ⟦ G ⟧cfg, otherwise inhabit the rejection side.

If the input is c ∷ w, recursively parse (δ c G) w via the syntactic derivative. Using ⟜ as derivative, a positive answer ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg w reshapes to ⟦ G ⟧cfg (c ∷ w); a negative answer ¬ ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg w lifts to ¬ ⟦ G ⟧cfg (c ∷ w).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Well-foundedness: on each recursive call length w strictly decreases. The grammar may grow (derivatives of CFGs are unbounded), but the well-founded relation is on the input, not the state. This mirrors how GCD.<₂-wellFounded in the intrinsically-recursive paper is well-founded on proj₂ of the index, not on the full index.
Concretely, the recursion uses <-wellFounded on ℕ via Cubical.Induction.WellFounded (already imported by the project's dependency on agda-stdlib).

This tree defines the algorithm operationally. The next step, parser as c2a-morphism, reinterprets the same definition as a unique coalgebra-to-algebra morphism, so the correctness proof becomes a uniqueness argument rather than a direct induction.
Milestone: implement this first for a hand-rolled Dyck (bypassing CFGDesc for the moment) to shake out the ⟜/nullability gymnastics before trying to generalise.

fr:title.text: Linear Residual ⟜ as Brzozowski Derivative

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Grammar.LinearFunction.Base, the right residual is (A ⟜ B) w = ∀ (w' : String) → B w' → A (w' ++ w). Reading this at a single-character grammar char c we get
(G ⟜ char c) w = ∀ w' → (char c) w' → G (w' ++ w) ≅ G (c ∷ w),
i.e. the Brzozowski derivative of G by c, up to the canonical iso char c · w ≅ c ∷ w for singleton matches.

So the calculus already has a semantic notion of derivative as a type constructor, not just as an operation on descriptions. The syntactic derivative δ c G should then denote exactly ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c, and the Brzozowski adjointness c · G ≅ δ c G is an instance of the tensor/residual adjunction char c · G ⊢ H ⟺ G ⊢ H ⟜ char c.
Why this matters for the plan:

html:ul.html:li: It grounds δ in the calculus rather than treating it as an external device: δ c G = G ⟜ char c already has the right type.
It means the parser's recursive structure can be phrased internally as currying over char c · - / uncurrying over - ⟜ char c, without leaving the calculus.
It suggests CFGDesc may not need ⟜ as a primitive — the operator can live outside the description as long as we can compute δ on descriptions and prove ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ≅ ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open question: for grammars with nullable residuals the adjunction interacts with the nullability gating in δ c (G · H); make sure the semantic direction of the iso stays available in both cases. This is tracked in risks.

fr:title.text: Syntactic Derivatives on CFGDesc

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a character c : Alphabet and a description G : CFGDesc, define a description δ c G : CFGDesc and a morphism at the semantics
deriv c G : char c · ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⊢ ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ,
together with an inverse deriv⁻¹ c G : ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ⊢ char c · ⟦ G ⟧cfg , so the pair witnesses the Brzozowski identity c · G ≅ δ c G inside grammar (not language) semantics.
Regex case is classical:

html:ul.html:li: δ c ε = ⊥;
δ c (char a) = if a ≟ c then ε else ⊥;
δ c (G · H) = (δ c G) · H ⊕ ν? G · δ c H, where ν? gates the second summand by nullability;
δ c (G ⊕ H) = δ c G ⊕ δ c H;
δ c (G *) = δ c G · G *.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For μ we unfold once before deriving, using the productivity side condition to ensure the derivative terminates at the description level (the description does not grow under δ past a bounded residual form). This is the part most likely to need care — see risks.

CFG derivatives in general (Might, Darais, Spiewak 2011) form an infinite but regular-in-the-right-sense family; the reachable derivative states for a given G correspond to the states of a PDA for G. We do not need finitely many residuals; we only need each derivative to be well-typed and to decrease the string length we feed it.

For Dyck specifically, the derivative by LP moves us to a state "expecting one extra RP before completion", and iterating gives the unbounded stack. The state space is infinite; the per-string computation is still well-founded on input length, which is where well-founded recursion on length comes in.

fr:title.text: Decidable Nullability for CFGDesc

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For every description G : CFGDesc, we want a decision nullable? G : Bool with proofs

html:ul.html:li: nullable? G ≡ true → NullableG ⟦ G ⟧cfg;
nullable? G ≡ false → ¬Nullable ⟦ G ⟧cfg.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: NullableG A = ε & A and ¬Nullable_ already live in Grammar.SequentialUnambiguity.Nullable. They are "second-class" (external propositions, not a type-level decoration), but they give exactly the lemmas we need: ¬Nullable⊗l, ¬Nullable⊗r, and the char⁺ equivalence.
Inductive clauses (following the RE pattern):

Decidable nullability is what makes the syntactic derivative total — for G · H the derivative splits into (δ G) · H (always) plus δ H guarded by nullable? G, and without the decision we cannot form that sum.

This is also where the paper's well-foundedness shows up syntactically: requiring every μ-body to force a character (non-nullable prefix) is the statement that the derived base functor is guarded in the sense of the guard functor ↓₀.

fr:title.text: CFGDesc: Embedded Syntax of Guarded CFGs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: CFGDesc: Embedded Syntax of Guarded CFGs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The first ingredient of the plan is a data type CFGDesc describing a class of grammars closed under the operations we need, for which nullability and derivatives can be computed syntactically.

Mirrors Grammar.RegularExpression.Base.RegularExpression and its denotation ⟦ _ ⟧r. The regex case is a useful template because the syntactic structure is what makes derivative-based parsing work: we can induct on the description while the semantics does not support such induction in general.
Sketch of constructors:

html:ul.html:li: ε, ⊥, char a (atoms);
_·_ (tensor), _⊕_ (alternation), _* (Kleene star);

μ (fixed points) — the CFG extension over regexes — with a productivity side condition (every self-reference must occur under a non-nullable prefix). This mirrors how the intrinsically-recursive paper uses non-nullable tensors to get a guarded list / tree functor.
⟜ and ⊸ — tentatively, to match the linear-residual derivative.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The productivity/guardedness side condition is the syntactic counterpart of the paper's well-foundedness of the base functor. Intended denotation: ⟦ _ ⟧cfg : CFGDesc → Grammar ℓ-zero (exactly as for regexes).

The Dyck language is representable as μ D. ε ⊕ (LP · D · RP · D), where both recursive occurrences sit under non-nullable LP. This is the first concrete witness that the productivity condition admits the grammars we care about.
Downstream this tree is consumed by:

html:ul.html:li: Decidable nullability;
Syntactic derivatives;
Parser construction.

fr:title.text: Plan: Derivative-Based CFG Parser via Recursive Coalgebras

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Plan: Derivative-Based CFG Parser via Recursive Coalgebras

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A concrete path for exercising well-founded recursive coalgebras in dep-Lambek: build a generic derivative-based parser for a syntactically-delimited class of context-free grammars, in direct analogy with the existing regular-expression infrastructure (Grammar.RegularExpression). Every step should admit a compositional, well-founded account, and the whole thing should ultimately factor through the c2a-morph theorem of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint].

The Dyck language serves as the running test: it is not regular, its derivatives form an infinite (PDA-shaped) state space, and it cannot admit a map string ⊢ Dyck — only a Parser Dyck ¬Dyck. We want to derive the automaton shape, not assume it.
The phases:

html:ol.html:li: CFGDesc: an embedded syntax of guarded CFGs.
Decidable nullability for CFGDesc.
Syntactic derivatives on CFGDesc.
Linear residual ⟜ as Brzozowski derivative.
Parser by well-founded recursion on string length.
Parser as unique c2a-morphism of a recursive coalgebra.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Risks and open questions are tracked in sss-00AA.
An orthogonal re-foundation that would internalise phases 2 and 5 into the type system is discussed in Later operator ▶ as internalised guard.

First concrete deliverable: a hand-coded Dyck parser at the semantic level (outside CFGDesc) that matches what the generic pipeline should later produce automatically. Only then do we generalise to CFGDesc.

Execution track in progress: Finish derivative-based parsing on brzozowski. The brzozowski branch already has the derivative machinery and a regex derivative operator with soundness; the Zippy LL(1) description type is also present. Closing the existing holes and building the regex + LL(1) parsers is phases 1–3 of this plan for a narrower grammar class.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Exploratory follow-up to sss-00B9. Once the suffix-flavoured ▷ (sss-00BC) is established and Löb (sss-00BE) is settled, repeat the construction for the prefix variant (mostly mechanical), then attempt the proper-substring variant.

html:ol.html:li: Direct: define ▷ˢᵘᵇ A = &[ w ∈ NonEmptyString ] (⊤ ⊗ string w ⊗ ⊤) ⇒ (⊤ ⊗ string w ⊗ A ⊗ ⊤) or some variant; pick the side on which A lands carefully.

Resolution (2026-04-29). Built as Grammar/Later/Substring.agda on the guarded branch of the gsa-brzozowski worktree. The chosen formulation is bilateral peeling: index over NonEmptyPair = Σ u, v. (u, v) ≢ ([], []), with each component \sqrt [u,v]{A} \;=\; {\mathopen {}\left (\texttt {String}\, u \otimes \top \otimes \texttt {String}\, v\right )\mathclose {}} \;\Rightarrow \; {\mathopen {}\left (\texttt {String}\, u \otimes A \otimes \texttt {String}\, v\right )\mathclose {}}. Löb induction goes through by the same well-founded-on-length recursion as the suffix case, since in any decomposition w'' \equiv u\, s\, v with (u, v) \neq (\epsilon , \epsilon ) the middle s is strictly shorter than w''. fr:title.text: Resolution: next is structure, not a theorem

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Resolution: next is structure, not a theorem

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The diagram chase does not go through for arbitrary grammars — the verification check anticipated above fails. next is not derivable from the indexed-product definition of ▷ alone; it requires extra structure on A.

Max's framing. Presheaves on (\texttt {String}, \text {suffix-order}) are precisely \Box -coalgebras over families. The map next : A ⊢ ▷ A is the coalgebra structure, not a global term. So instead of postulating it (or holding it open as a hole), package it as a record:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: record IsCoalgebra (A : Grammar ℓA) : Type ℓA where field next : A ⊢ ▷ A
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The canonical example is ⊤-IsCoalgebra: ⊤ is suffix-closed because any suffix of a ⊤-parse is a ⊤-parse. This lives in Grammar/Later/Coalgebra.agda on the guarded branch of gsa-brzozowski.

html:ul.html:li: Grammar/Later/Base.agda now compiles without --allow-unsolved-metas — the held-open next hole is gone.
Löb (sss-00BE) goes through unchanged: the obstruction to next does not block Löb, because Löb is proven directly by well-founded recursion on string length and never invokes a global next.

This is the same shape of design discovery as Cass's recursive-coalgebra framework: well-foundedness + recursion lives on coalgebra structures, not on bare grammars. The connection is made explicit in the recursive-coalgebra synthesis — next is the coalgebra structure that feeds a c2a-morphism.

fr:title.text: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What the bookkeeping is over: unsolved metas, not an elaborated term

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Removing --allow-unsolved-metas from Real04 fails with [UnsolvedConstraints]. Same for RealFlat04. So with --lossy-unification on, Agda doesn't actually finish elaborating the proof. The body persisted to the interface is a single reference to an unsolved meta (unsolvedmeta.N) parameterised by the module's level args. The "elaborated term" I attributed the cost to in earlier drafts of this tree doesn't exist.

What does exist in the meta-store: 384 unsolved metas for Real04, 174 for RealFlat04, 73 for Real00. Each unsolved meta carries a type, a context (telescope of variables in scope), and entries on Agda's constraint list. With lossy on, Agda gives up on the trickier ones rather than recursing forever, and they remain in the store. The 11.5s of bookkeeping is over those 384 meta entries, each of which has a SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_]-flavoured type that mentions g*Xᴰ = isFibrationSETᴰ._*_ g Xᴰ, the cartesian-product-fibration combinator, LRⱽObᴰ→LRⱽ, etc.
Direct AST measurements on the postulated-type fixtures (which DO fully elaborate, no unsolved metas) — by reflection in Bench/ReindFillerChains/SizeReflect.agda:

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two things stand out. First, on postulated types, term size grows quadratically with chain depth — 31k nodes at depth 32. Second, none of that matters for time: those cases all check in under 1s, dominated by interface-deserialization. So size alone is not the cost driver.

The cost driver is the meta store, not the elaborated term. Each Implicit/Wrapped AST node is R.def (quote postulate) — trivial for downstream passes to look up, highlight, serialize, and the postulated fixtures fully elaborate so no metas are left behind. In the real SETᴰ setting, the analogous pieces reference deep qualified names inside the displayed-presheaf infrastructure, the unifier under lossy gives up rather than recursing, and 384 entries remain in the meta store. The cost decomposes as
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: where the "unifier work per call" factor is what --lossy-unification bounds at typing time, and the bookkeeping passes (InverseNameLookup, Highlighting, Serialization, Miscellaneous) walk the remaining (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}) entries post-typing. Each lever attacks a different factor and they compose multiplicatively — see the annotation experiment below for the quantitative split.

The plateau on depth (Real04=13.0s, Real16=13.4s, Real32=14.1s, Real64=14.8s — ~30ms per junction past 4) is consistent: each extra junction adds one meta with similar type complexity, so the per-junction cost is small relative to the fixed cost of the wrapping itself.

fr:title.text: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why displayed presheaves are catastrophically worse

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same wrapping pattern, applied to displayed presheaves, has each junction's Hom-type be a NatTrans (component functions + naturality). Per-meta type complexity is multiplicatively bigger. Bookkeeping cost is (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}), so the displayed-presheaf case scales worse along the type-complexity axis even at the same chain depth.

fr:title.text: Verdict on the original hypothesis

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The comment in Sets/Properties.agda hypothesised that the slowness comes from "the unification of the implicit arguments to each of these reind fillers… we may mitigate the slowness here by removing nested reindexings." Sharper picture now:

html:ul.html:li: Right that unification is implicated and type-driven. 213s without --lossy-unification on the depth-4 chain; postulated-type fixtures (Wrapped, Implicit, Explicit) cannot reproduce the slowness even at depth 32 (31,334 AST nodes), so the cost is in unifying real SETᴰ.Hom[_][_,_] types, not in the chain shape itself.

Right that filling implicits helps — but the path argument, not the type implicits. Filling {a, b, p} on every reind-filler⁻ (the Explicit fixture) doesn't move the postulated case, which was already fast. But replacing the e : a ≡ b path argument with refl on the real chain gives a 2× speedup (13.13s → 6.20s on the bench, 14.83s → 6.75s in the actual library) by short-circuiting the unifier search at each reind-filler⁻ call.

Wrong about "nested reindexings" being the lever. Cutting nesting depth only saves ~30ms per junction past depth 4 — Real04≈Real16 ≈Real64 under lossy. The proof shape's chain length is not what's expensive.

The dominant residual cost is bookkeeping over the meta store. With lossy on, typing is 1.3 percent of the total; the remaining 11.5s is post-typing work over 384 unsolved metas, set by (\text {meta count}) \times (\text {per-meta type complexity}). Lossy and explicit-refl attack the typing factor; strictification is what attacks per-meta type complexity (and shrinks the bookkeeping bill proportionally).

fr:title.text: Decision on Yoneda strictification

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Yoneda strictification is still the right fix, with a sharper reason than the original comment suggested. The win is not "the unifier sees fewer reduction obligations". The win is "each unsolved meta in the store has a smaller, simpler type", because the strictified fiber types substituted into each junction are smaller. The downstream bookkeeping passes (scope lookup, highlighting, interface build) walk those meta types and shrink proportionally.

Concrete prediction: strictification should drop Real04 from ~13s back toward Real00's ~3.4s import baseline, mostly by collapsing the Miscellaneous + InverseNameLookup + Highlighting + Serialization buckets, not the Typing bucket (which is already small under lossy).

It will not eliminate the import cost (Real00 is 3.4s with the current import graph, almost entirely in deserialization) — that's a separate concern about the size of the displayed-presheaf infrastructure being pulled in.

It does not obviate --lossy-unification: removing lossy turns the depth-4 case into 213s. The three levers attack different factors of (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) and are independent:

html:ul.html:li: --lossy-unification bounds unifier work per call (16×).
_ → refl annotation further cuts unifier work per call on top of lossy (2× more).
Strictification shrinks per-meta type complexity, which feeds through to both the typing cost and the post-typing bookkeeping.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: All three should be applied together. Strictification is the most invasive but addresses the largest single multiplier and the only one that touches the bookkeeping bill.

fr:mainmatter.html:pre: cost ≈ (meta count) × (per-meta type complexity) × (unifier work per call) ↑ ↑ ↑ (mostly fixed (lossy attacks (annotation attacks by proof shape) this; strictifi- this) cation also)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Practical take: in real Properties.agda code, the easy mechanical intervention reind-filler⁻ _ → reind-filler⁻ refl (where applicable) should give about a 2× speedup. It does not obviate --lossy-unification or strictification — those still own the bigger factors.

This explains the user's prior empirical observation: running C-u C-u C-c C-s (Solve constraints at strongest normalization) on ? holes returns refl-shaped solutions that, when written back into the source, give exactly this 2× speedup. fr:title.text: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Fibrations into a 1-category of groupoid-object categories

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Explore a streamlined setup for logical relations: work with a small category \mathcal {GC} whose objects are categories equipped with a groupoid object (or, equivalently, categories in which every map is invertible in the relevant sense), and whose morphisms are the appropriate structure-preserving functors. Define fibrations as functors into \mathcal {GC}. Because each fiber is a groupoid-enriched 1-category, \mathcal {GC} itself is a 1-category — there are no higher coherences to manage.

Motivation. The current displayed-category machinery in Finishing Logical Relations on Display spends a lot of effort on coherences that evaporate once the fibers are forced to be (truncated to) groupoidal. If the target 1-category is rich enough to express the constructions needed for canonicity and normalization logical relations, this may be a lighter foundation than the thickened / displayed-double-category route.

html:ol.html:li: Define the small 1-category \mathcal {GC} of categories-with-groupoid-objects and verify it is a 1-category (no higher cells).
Define fibrations as functors E \to \mathcal {GC} and relate them to the displayed-category presentation already in the library.
Encode the universal properties needed for semantics: terminal / binary products / exponentials at the base, plus their fiberwise analogues.
Encode universal quantification (right adjoint to pullback / reindexing) internally to this framework.
State and prove Beck--Chevalley for the relevant pullback squares.
State and prove Frobenius reciprocity for the left-adjoint / existential direction.
Reconstruct the canonicity logical relation in this framework as a first test case.
Reconstruct the normalization logical relation in this framework as a harder stress test.

html:ul.html:li: What exactly is the right notion of "groupoid object" here — an internal groupoid, a hom-groupoid enrichment, or truncation of hom-sets to sets? The choice affects whether \mathcal {GC} is genuinely small.
Does the 1-categorical structure survive once we add the universal-quantifier / Beck--Chevalley / Frobenius data, or do higher coherences creep back in through the adjoints?
How does this compare to the displayed-category-with-isos setup in Cubical/Categories/Displayed/ and the thickened displayed categories of PR 253?

fr:title.text: Sketch: the CFG derivative parser internal to LambekD

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sketch: the CFG derivative parser internal to LambekD

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Feasibility sketch for building the inductive derivative parser inside Lambek^{D} in Agda. The claim: it is definable and provable by combining the regex \delta + soundness on the brzozowski branch with \rhd /lob on the box branch; the one design decision is to put the guard in the datatype, and the one genuine risk is refl-time computation. Signatures below are schematic — proofs are holes, never postulates.

fr:title.text: Datatype: guard as a structural invariant

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Datatype: guard as a structural invariant

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The naive recursion δ c (var X) = δ c (def X) does not pass Agda's termination checker — def X is not a subterm and the keystone short-circuit is semantic. So encode the guard structurally, Greibach-style: a nonterminal is its finite list of guarded clauses ⌈c⌉ ⊗ tail.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
NT : Type -- finite context of nonterminals (e.g. Fin n)
data CFGDesc : Type where ⟨I⟩ ⟨⊥⟩ : CFGDesc -- ε , empty lit : ⟨ Alphabet ⟩ → CFGDesc -- ⌈c⌉ var : NT → CFGDesc -- nonterminal leaf _⊗_ _⊕_ : CFGDesc → CFGDesc → CFGDesc
record Production : Type where -- one nonterminal's productions field nullable : Bool -- is ε accepted? clauses : List (Alphabet × CFGDesc) -- guarded: (leading char , tail)
def : NT → Production -- the grammar = a table of productions
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The invariant "every var occurs behind a consumed terminal" is now unforgeable: a nonterminal reaches you only via a clauses entry, whose head is a literal. Unguarded grammars are not expressible.

fr:title.text: Nullability and derivative: both structural, Agda-accepted

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Nullability and derivative: both structural, Agda-accepted

fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
ν? : CFGDesc → Bool ν? ⟨I⟩ = true ν? ⟨⊥⟩ = false ν? (lit _) = false ν? (var X) = Production.nullable (def X) -- lookup, NOT recursive ν? (A ⊗ B) = ν? A and ν? B ν? (A ⊕ B) = ν? A or ν? B
δ : Alphabet → CFGDesc → CFGDesc δ c ⟨I⟩ = ⟨⊥⟩ δ c ⟨⊥⟩ = ⟨⊥⟩ δ c (lit c′) = if c == c′ then ⟨I⟩ else ⟨⊥⟩ δ c (A ⊕ B) = δ c A ⊕ δ c B δ c (A ⊗ B) = δ c A ⊗ B ⊕ (if ν? A then δ c B else ⟨⊥⟩) -- MUST short-circuit δ c (var X) = select c (Production.clauses (def X)) -- filter+strip, NO δ recursion where select c = foldr (λ (c′ , t) acc → if c == c′ then t ⊕ acc else acc) ⟨⊥⟩
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Both are structural recursions on CFGDesc: ν? (var X) and δ c (var X) are lookups, not recursive calls, so the termination checker is satisfied and the keystone is discharged by construction. CFGDesc is visibly closed under δ (residuals mention var, never a differentiated nonterminal).

fr:title.text: Semantics, soundness, and the parser

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Interpret into grammars — var as the guarded fixpoint (this is where the datatype's guard earns its keep, making the \mu well-defined via lob) — and prove the Brzozowski iso by induction on CFGDesc, its var case discharged by one \mu -unfold. Then the generic Löb parser.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
⟦_⟧ : CFGDesc → Grammar -- var ↦ μ (guarded), ⊗/⊕/lit/I/⊥ pointwise
δ-sound : (c : Alphabet)(G : CFGDesc) → ⟦ δ c G ⟧ ≅ ⟦ G ⟧ ⟜ lit c δ-sound c G = {!!} -- induction on G; var: μ-unfold + guard
Ans : CFGDesc → Grammar Ans G = ⟦ G ⟧ ⊕ ¬ ⟦ G ⟧
parse : (G : CFGDesc) → ⊤ ⊢ Ans G parse = lob λ rec G → {!!} -- ⊤ ≅ I ⊕ ⊕[c] ⌈c⌉ ⊗ ▷⊤ ; at I: ν? G ; at ⌈c⌉⊗▷: transport (rec (δ c G))
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The parse hole needs only: the guarded string decomposition of \top (box branch), the \rhd -guard discharge for the recursive call (⌈c⌉ ⊗ (−) factors through \rhd , sss-00EX), and δ-sound to move the answer across. Totality and correctness are then lob's uniqueness.

fr:title.text: The real risk: does it compute?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The real risk: does it compute?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Type-checking and proofs are the easy direction. Reducing parse dyck "aabb" by refl is the wall, and the constraints are known:

html:ul.html:li: lob reduces by refl only in Eq-world — the well-founded order must be Eq-valued or löbWF sticks under transp (reference: the Eq-vs-transp Löb issue).
Tensors must be SplittingEq from the start, or the hcomp/path-Splittings blowup that stalled witness evaluation returns.
Derivative descriptions grow; compaction (generic \bot /I unit rewrites) is optional for correctness but may be load-bearing for computation.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Empirically Dyck-style refl-evaluation was made tractable this way, while regex/greedy parsers did not terminate — so Dyck at refl is the first target; a general CFGDesc interpreter that computes is the open question, not a definability one.

html:ol.html:li: CFGDesc + Production datatype (guard structural), over the project's Alphabet.
ν?, δ (structural, total — no holes; termination free from the encoding).
⟦_⟧ and δ-sound (holes; induction on CFGDesc, reusing the brzozowski regex soundness pattern).
parse = lob … (hole; reuses box lob + \rhd decomposition).
Dyck instance; attempt refl-evaluation in Eq-world + SplittingEq; add compaction only if size blows up.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Steps 1–2 are self-contained and hole-free; 3–4 are the real proof work; 5 is the empirical gate. Reuses, does not rebuild, sss-00A6/sss-00A7 (regex \delta + soundness) and sss-00BE/sss-00BD (\rhd /lob).

fr:title.text: A ranked-container interface for hylomorphisms

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Package the functor and its contractive strength as a ranked container / well-founded signature: shapes S x, positions Pos s, and an assignment of each position to a strictly-smaller index (the rank), so the functor is H₀ A x = Σ (s : S x) → Π (p : Pos s) → A (idx s p) with idx s p ≺ x. The strength is then generic.
The container was retired once in favour of an inline functor plus a two-line δ (which was lighter); the request is a clean optional interface, not a forced encoding.
This is the well-founded, single-sorted special case of the grammar indexed-inductive functor.

fr:title.text: Compositional combinators for local contractivity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every hylomorphism example currently hand-writes its functor and its contractive strength (the δ). Local contractivity should instead be a closed class with combinators, so larger contractive maps are assembled from smaller ones and δ is derived.
The closure conditions --- the guarded/metric semantics of the later modality:

html:ul.html:li: constant functors are contractive;
a recursive position guarded by \triangleright is contractive --- a bare variable is only non-expansive;
sums, products, and linear/tensor products preserve contractivity positionwise;
composition with a non-expansive functor preserves contractivity on either side.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are exactly the constructors of the grammar functor language, which is a syntactic form of this calculus. Pairs with the ranked-container interface.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes from a meeting with Max about strictification, wrapping up conservativity for the Logical Relations on Display paper, and chasing the source of slowness in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties.

Three layers of strictification are now on the table. The ExtraId category buys judgmental \mathrm {IdL} for free. A Yoneda strictification of the base — taking morphisms to be PshHomStrict between representables — promotes both unitors and associativity to refl. Pushing the same trick one level up, by replacing the elements of a presheaf P with PshHomStrict from the Yoneda embedding into P, makes F-id and F-seq of every presheaf definitional too.

Open question: what survives the strictification? The library's existing constructions and logical relations live over the non-strict base. We need to articulate how the strictified versions relate back — i.e., how the same logical relations are extracted from a proof done over the strict side. This is the same boundary cost flagged in the Yoneda strictification tradeoffs note; the answer is what determines whether strictification is worth integrating versus running as a private experiment.

Conservativity for the paper. The current presented-lambda conservativity proof is split across two steps; Max suggests fusing them by proving fullness through an extensional universal property directly. If the strictification experiments work out, including them gives a more direct comparison to Kaposi--Pujet and corroborates their strictification observations.

Plan for the strictification experiments. (i) Identify the minimal amount of library code that would need to be duplicated or rewritten over a strict base. (ii) Verify the vector of slowness — strictification only helps if the cost actually lives in unitor/associator reindexing. (iii) Build the strict version, conditional on (i) and (ii) being favorable.

Slowness measurement. The slowness is concentrated in Displayed.Instances.Sets.Properties: vertical exponentials and the universal quantifier over the displayed sets category typecheck pathologically slowly despite simple goals. Working hypothesis (consistent with the slow filler chains note and the hcomp speedup note): the cost is the depth of nested reindexings combined with the filler-at-a-time proof style, where many of the offending transports are over refl. Tracked separately as a benchmark TODO — gates the broader strictification decision.

fr:title.text: Well-foundedness of the Dyck functor via the string-decomposition axiom

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Well-foundedness of the Dyck functor via the string-decomposition axiom

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Context: the well-foundedness sense here is the one in [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint], and the tie-in with well-founded recursive coalgebras in dep-Lambek is the reason for caring.
The Dyck functor. Consider the polynomial functor
and let D be its initial F-algebra, so D \simeq I \oplus \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"} \otimes D \otimes \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"} \otimes D.

The string-decomposition axiom. In dep-Lambek we have the axiom \top \simeq \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \lceil w \rceil which internalizes the external reasoning on strings: every top-element is quoted as some specific w. Equivalently \top \simeq {\mathtt {Char}}^{*} \quad \text {where} \quad \mathtt {Char} = \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (c : \mathcal {A}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \texttt {"}c\texttt {"}.

Decomposing D. Using the axiom we can refine D into an indexed sum over explicit sub-strings. Peeling off one constructor and inserting a quote for each recursive occurrence gives D \simeq I \oplus \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left ({\mathopen {}\left (w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2\right )\mathclose {}}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (\lceil w_1 \rceil \mathrel {\And } D\right )\mathclose {}} \otimes \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"} \otimes {\mathopen {}\left (\lceil w_2 \rceil \mathrel {\And } D\right )\mathclose {}}.

Because w = \texttt {"}lp\texttt {"}\, w_1\, \texttt {"}rp\texttt {"}\, w_2, we know |w_1|, |w_2| < |w|. The well-foundedness argument is now visible in the type: the recursive D occurrences are guarded by shorter quoted strings.

Reading. The string-decomposition axiom is doing all of the work of externally reasoning about string length. Everything that normally lives "on paper" — inducting on |w|, case-splitting on the first character — is now accessible internally through the quote types \lceil - \rceil and the \oplus /\mathrel {\And } structure. See also the trivial-case question for the related \top vs. \lceil w \rceil puzzle in the guarded setting.

fr:title.text: Candidates for a guarded modality in dep-Lambek

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Candidates for a guarded modality in dep-Lambek

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Related: Can I use guarded recursion?, well-founded recursion in dep-Lambek.

Analytic candidate. Internally a grammar is essentially A : \mathrm {String} \to \mathbb {N} \to \mathbf {Set}, and we could set {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, 0 = \top , \qquad {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, {\mathopen {}\left (\mathsf {suc}\, n\right )\mathclose {}} = A\, w\, n. This is the usual step-indexed later: shift the index by one and give free truth at step zero.

Synthetic candidate. In Agda we could alternatively define {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w = \triangleright \, {\mathopen {}\left (A\, w\right )\mathclose {}} and inherit the ambient later modality of the synthetic guarded type theory. This keeps grammar-indexing orthogonal to step-indexing.

Open question. Which of these plays best with the Dyck functor / string-decomposition story? The analytic version makes step-indexing and string-length arguments interact explicitly; the synthetic version defers that to the ambient modality but needs to be reconciled with the grammar-as-type-family structure. See also the trivial-case question.

fr:title.text: Trivial case of the guarded modality: should it be top or the current string's quote?

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Trivial case of the guarded modality: should it be top or the current string's quote?

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pre-meeting notes for the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Branch of guarded modality candidates for Lambek^{D}{}.

The puzzle. In the usual guarded setting, \triangleright A at step 0 gives back \top . But in the Lambek^{D}{} setting we have access to the current string w. I suspect the trivial case should bottom out at \lceil w \rceil rather than \top : {\mathopen {}\left (\triangleright A\right )\mathclose {}}\, w\, 0 \;\stackrel {?}{=}\; \lceil w \rceil . The intuition: at step 0 we've consumed exactly the string w, so the "trivial" proposition is that the string we have is w, not an unconstrained \top .

Tension with the string-decomposition axiom. However, the axiom \top \simeq \mathchoice {\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\textstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}{\scriptscriptstyle \oplus _{{\mathopen {}\left (w : \mathrm {String}\right )\mathclose {}}}}\, \lceil w \rceil (see the Dyck well-foundedness note) already equates \top with a big-\oplus of quotes. Under a fixed w these may collapse: \top restricted to w already is \lceil w \rceil . So the question may be cosmetic — the two presentations might be isomorphic — but the \lceil w \rceil form is likely the one that carries the right definitional equalities for proofs.
To discuss: which form plays better with well-founded recursion and with recursive-descent-as-unfold?

fr:title.text: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Subterm ordering and the inverse of the initial algebra as a recursive coalgebra

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. See also well-founded recursion in dep-Lambek and derivative-based CFG parser via recursive coalgebras.

Cass's suggestion. For an initial F-algebra D, there is an evident subterm ordering on D. The inverse of the initial algebra is a coalgebra structure on D, and it might be possible to show that this coalgebra is well-founded with respect to that subterm ordering — obtaining a recursive-coalgebra witness without going through the final coalgebra.

Stronger claim to check. Cass further suggested that the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, even when it is not the final coalgebra. The approach rests on this claim, and it needs to be verified — dig into the coalgebra literature (Adámek, Capretta, Uustalu, Vene) for the precise statement.

Why this matters. If true, it gives a categorical justification for recursive definitions on initial algebras like the Dyck grammar without invoking step-indexing or guarded modalities. It would complement — or replace — the guarded-modality candidates as the well-foundedness mechanism.

fr:title.text: Recursive-descent parsers as unfolds

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22.

Max's claim. Recursive-descent parsers cannot be written in a terminating way directly. The fix may be to write them as an unfold (anamorphism / coalgebra map) rather than a fold: the parser is characterised not as a recursive function into a syntax tree, but as a map out of the input stream via a coalgebra structure on the state.

This dovetails with the recursive-coalgebra framing — recursive descent becomes the unique map from the initial/input coalgebra into an F-coalgebra for the grammar's functor. The derivative-based CFG parser plan already walks in this direction.

Concrete takeaway for LL(1). The LL(1) goal (see finishing the deterministic regex code) is the first place to try this: once the grammar functor and its coalgebra-of-derivatives are pinned down, the parser is the unfold, and termination falls out of well-foundedness rather than structural recursion on the input.

fr:title.text: Lexing as morphisms between alphabet literals

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lexing as morphisms between alphabet literals

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Tangential thought.

The hope. If we allow morphisms between the generating data of Lambek^{D}{} — i.e. between the literals \texttt {"}c\texttt {"} for c : \mathcal {A} — then lexing can be encoded internally: a lexer is just a morphism \texttt {"}c_1\texttt {"} \to \texttt {"}c_2\texttt {"} (or more precisely a morphism between the generated grammars of raw characters and token classes). Traditional categorial grammar does something like this.

Max's pitfall. Having morphisms between generators creates an obligation to be natural with respect to them. That constrains every construction in the calculus and may be a total roadblock — I am unsure.

Possible escape route. There may be an interesting use of tinyness (right adjoints that preserve colimits for size reasons) to escape the naturality obligation in the places that matter. Worth a separate investigation after the core guarded/well-foundedness story stabilises.

fr:title.text: Monadic parser combinators as chains of isos, and the "Dijkstra monad"

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Monadic parser combinators as chains of isos, and the "Dijkstra monad"

fr:mainmatter.html:p: From the advisor meeting on 2026-04-22. Tangential thought.

Observation. Monadic parser combinators feel like they are naively written via chains of isomorphisms, where each iso relates to the iso between a string and A \oplus \neg A for a complete parser (since a complete parser maps the input into either a grammar A or its complement). This is structurally reminiscent of how quantum languages are forced to invoke chains of isos.

Snag. In the Lambek^{D}{} setting a parser combinator written this naive way cannot be proven terminating directly — the same pathology as recursive descent. But the same escape hatch (well-foundedness via recursive coalgebras or guarded modality) should apply.

The "Dijkstra monad" puzzle. We accumulate complement types as the combinators compose — a sort of negation monad. Ohad called this something like a "Dijkstra monad" a while back. I have not found this nomenclature elsewhere in writing. Action item: ask on Mastodon for the reference.
